attribution: Sugar contents are typical values for ripe fruit, cross-checked against the USDA FoodData Central composition tables; juice Brix, press yield, titratable acidity and pH are typical ranges from standard fruit-processing and winemaking references. Fruit is a biological product — cultivar, season, ripeness and growing site move these figures substantially, which is why minimum, typical and maximum are all given. Where you have a refractometer reading, use it in preference to any of these numbers.

fermentables.name: Apple (dessert)
fermentables.description: Standard eating apple. Low tannin and moderate acid, so on its own it makes a light, simple cider that benefits from blending.
fermentables.usageNotes: Pectin haze is near-certain without pectic enzyme. Supermarket juice is usually this profile.

fermentables.name: Apple (bittersweet cider variety)
fermentables.description: True cider apples: high tannin, low acid, largely inedible fresh. The soft-tannin backbone of West Country and Normandy cider.
fermentables.usageNotes: Low acid means a blend with sharps is usually needed to get pH under 3.8. Low nitrogen — these are the varieties that keeve.

fermentables.name: Apple (bittersharp cider variety)
fermentables.description: The rare varieties carrying both acid and tannin — the ones that can make a complete single-varietal cider.
fermentables.usageNotes: Kingston Black is the classic vintage-quality apple; it also ferments notoriously unreliably.

fermentables.name: Apple (sharp / culinary)
fermentables.description: Cooking apples. High malic acid, negligible tannin — a blending component that props up the pH of a bittersweet-heavy blend.
fermentables.usageNotes: Useful for correcting a flabby low-acid must without reaching for the acid packet.

fermentables.name: Crabapple
fermentables.description: Wild or ornamental apple: small, fiercely acidic and astringent, and much higher in pectin than a dessert apple.
fermentables.usageNotes: A little goes a long way as a tannin and acid correction. Expect a hard, slow press.

fermentables.name: Pear (dessert)
fermentables.description: Eating pear. Contains sorbitol, which yeast cannot ferment — so a pear ferment finishes dry on paper and still tastes sweet.
fermentables.usageNotes: The Williams pear is the basis of Poire Williams eau-de-vie. High pH: acidify toward 3.5 before pitching.

fermentables.name: Perry Pear (traditional)
fermentables.description: Traditional perry pears — high tannin, high sorbitol, and often high citric acid, which invites lactic spoilage that apple rarely sees.
fermentables.usageNotes: Mill and leave the pomace to stand before pressing; unlike apple, fresh-milled perry pear presses poorly.

fermentables.name: Quince
fermentables.description: Hard, aromatic and inedible raw. Enormous pectin load and a perfume that survives fermentation better than most fruit.
fermentables.usageNotes: The highest-pectin fruit here — pectic enzyme is mandatory, and a fruit brandy from quince needs careful methanol cuts.

fermentables.name: Peach
fermentables.description: Delicate and easily lost. Most of what reads as peach in a finished beer or wine comes from yeast esters, not fruit.
fermentables.usageNotes: Add late and generously — 1–2 kg per 20 L is not excessive. Freeze and thaw first to break down cell walls.

fermentables.name: Nectarine
fermentables.description: A fuzzless peach, and effectively interchangeable with one in the fermenter.
fermentables.usageNotes: Same handling as peach: freeze, thaw, add post-primary.

fermentables.name: Apricot
fermentables.description: Much more acidic than peach and with a firmer aromatic signature that survives fermentation.
fermentables.usageNotes: Kernels contain amygdalin — do not crush the stones into the must in quantity.

fermentables.name: Plum (European)
fermentables.description: The base of slivovitz and quetsch. Skins carry real tannin and colour, and the sugar runs high in a good year.
fermentables.usageNotes: Ferment on the skins for colour. Destone before fermentation for spirit washes.

fermentables.name: Damson
fermentables.description: A small, astringent, intensely coloured plum. Too sharp to eat, excellent in a ferment.
fermentables.usageNotes: Pairs well with a sweeter base — damson alone will finish austere.

fermentables.name: Cherry (sweet)
fermentables.description: Dessert cherry — plenty of sugar, not much acid, and a pH high enough to need watching.
fermentables.usageNotes: Less suited to kriek than the tart types; the acid balance ends up flat.

fermentables.name: Cherry (tart / sour)
fermentables.description: The kriek cherry. Low sugar, high acid, and stone-and-skin tannin that gives a lambic its grip.
fermentables.usageNotes: Traditional kriek uses whole cherries with stones, macerated for months — the stones contribute a faint almond note.

fermentables.name: Mango
fermentables.description: High sugar, low acid, heavy pectin. Pulpy enough that it will not clear without help.
fermentables.usageNotes: pH is high enough that acidification is worth considering for a wine. Pectic enzyme essential.

fermentables.name: Strawberry
fermentables.description: Very low sugar for its bulk and notoriously fragile aroma — most of the character is lost to fermentation.
fermentables.usageNotes: Use at high rates and late. Colour fades to a dull orange-brown within months; this is normal and not spoilage.

fermentables.name: Raspberry
fermentables.description: Low sugar, high acid, and an aroma that survives fermentation better than almost any other berry.
fermentables.usageNotes: The framboise fruit. 1.5–2 kg per 20 L for a clear varietal character.

fermentables.name: Blackberry
fermentables.description: Seedy, tannic and deeply coloured. More structure than raspberry and a better candidate for a standalone wine.
fermentables.usageNotes: Seeds carry harsh tannin — press gently and avoid grinding them.

fermentables.name: Blueberry
fermentables.description: Higher sugar than the cane berries, with skin tannin and anthocyanin that shifts from purple to red as pH drops.
fermentables.usageNotes: Freeze before use to rupture the skins; whole blueberries in a fermenter give up very little.

fermentables.name: Elderberry
fermentables.description: The classic English country-wine berry: enormous colour, real tannin, and enough structure to age for years.
fermentables.usageNotes: Cook before use. Raw berries, and especially stems, leaves and unripe fruit, contain cyanogenic glycosides — strip the berries from the stems and heat them.

fermentables.name: Blackcurrant
fermentables.description: Ferociously acidic and tannic, with an aroma so strong it dominates anything it is blended into.
fermentables.usageNotes: Titratable acidity around 30 g/L means dilution or deacidification is not optional for a drinkable wine.

fermentables.name: Redcurrant
fermentables.description: Bright, sharp and pale. Needs both dilution and sugar to reach a fermentable balance.
fermentables.usageNotes: Very high pectin — expect a slow press and a stubborn haze.

fermentables.name: Gooseberry
fermentables.description: Sharp and green-tasting, with a thiol character that overlaps Sauvignon Blanc — which is why the tasting note exists.
fermentables.usageNotes: A traditional base for English sparkling country wine, where the high acid is an asset.

fermentables.name: Cranberry
fermentables.description: The most acidic common berry and among the most tannic. pH 2.5 will stall many yeasts outright.
fermentables.usageNotes: Blend or dilute heavily. On its own the must is below the pH most wine yeast will tolerate.

fermentables.name: Aronia (Chokeberry)
fermentables.description: The most astringent fruit in common use — polyphenol levels several times those of blueberry.
fermentables.usageNotes: Use as a colour and tannin adjunct rather than a base. Ages remarkably well.

fermentables.name: Mulberry
fermentables.description: Soft, sweet and staining. Low tannin and moderate acid make it an easy, if simple, ferment.
fermentables.usageNotes: Extremely perishable — freeze on picking.

fermentables.name: Boysenberry
fermentables.description: Raspberry–blackberry hybrids. Behave like blackberry with a touch more aromatic lift.
fermentables.usageNotes: Interchangeable with blackberry for planning purposes.

fermentables.name: Sea Buckthorn
fermentables.description: Extraordinarily acidic — roughly the titratable acidity of lemon juice — with an oily, sea-air aroma unlike anything else.
fermentables.usageNotes: Cannot be fermented undiluted. Treat as a flavouring at 5–10% of the must.

fermentables.name: Lingonberry
fermentables.description: Nordic bog berry: sharp, tannic and naturally high in benzoic acid, which resists spoilage and also slows yeast.
fermentables.usageNotes: The benzoic acid content can inhibit fermentation — pitch heavily and expect a slow start.

fermentables.name: Cloudberry
fermentables.description: Rare Nordic berry with a distinctive baked-apple and honey aroma.
fermentables.usageNotes: Scarce and expensive — usually used as a flavouring fraction rather than a base.

fermentables.name: Rosehip
fermentables.description: A traditional country-wine base, very high in pectin and vitamin C, with a mild floral-fruit character.
fermentables.usageNotes: The internal hairs are a serious irritant — use whole or strained, never crushed and unstrained.

fermentables.name: Grape (table)
fermentables.description: Eating grapes: less sugar and far less acid and tannin than wine varieties, bred for crunch rather than fermentation.
fermentables.usageNotes: Makes a thin wine on its own. Fine as a beer adjunct or a base for a neutral spirit wash.

fermentables.name: Grape (red wine variety, generic)
fermentables.description: Generic red vinifera at harvest ripeness. Use the varietal database for a specific grape.
fermentables.usageNotes: Ferment on skins for colour and tannin. 24 Brix is roughly 14% potential alcohol.

fermentables.name: Grape (white wine variety, generic)
fermentables.description: Generic white vinifera at harvest ripeness. Use the varietal database for a specific grape.
fermentables.usageNotes: Press off the skins immediately unless a skin-contact style is intended.

fermentables.name: Grape (Concord)
fermentables.description: The American native grape. Unmistakable 'foxy' methyl anthranilate aroma, high acid, and low sugar by vinifera standards.
fermentables.usageNotes: Almost always chaptalised. The foxy character is a varietal signature, not a fault.

fermentables.name: Orange
fermentables.description: Sweet orange. The juice ferments cleanly; most of the aroma people want is in the peel, not the flesh.
fermentables.usageNotes: For witbier and gin the dried bitter-orange peel is the traditional ingredient — see the botanicals catalog.

fermentables.name: Blood Orange
fermentables.description: Anthocyanin-pigmented orange with more acid and a raspberry edge to the aroma.
fermentables.usageNotes: The red pigment is pH-sensitive and largely lost in fermentation — expect colour disappointment.

fermentables.name: Lemon
fermentables.description: Effectively an acid source with a little sugar attached — around 48 g/L citric acid.
fermentables.usageNotes: Never a base. Use for acid correction or late aroma; the zest carries the limonene.

fermentables.name: Lime
fermentables.description: Even sharper than lemon. A gose and margarita-adjacent flavouring, not a fermentable.
fermentables.usageNotes: Pith turns bitter and vegetal in a long ferment — zest only, added late.

fermentables.name: Grapefruit
fermentables.description: Bitter as well as sour, from naringin in the pith and membranes — the bitterness carries into the finished drink.
fermentables.usageNotes: Overlaps heavily with the thiol character of Citra and Simcoe, which is why grapefruit IPAs work.

fermentables.name: Mandarin / Tangerine
fermentables.description: Sweeter and less acidic than orange, with a distinctly perfumed peel.
fermentables.usageNotes: The peel oil is the reason to use it — juice alone is unremarkable.

fermentables.name: Yuzu
fermentables.description: Aromatic Japanese citrus — mostly peel and seed, with a very low juice yield and a floral, grapefruit-mandarin nose.
fermentables.usageNotes: Expensive and worth using as zest or juice at low rates. 25% juice yield is optimistic for hand-pressing.

fermentables.name: Kumquat
fermentables.description: Eaten whole, peel and all — sweet skin, sour flesh. Fermented whole it gives both oil and acid.
fermentables.usageNotes: Halve and freeze before use; whole fruit floats and moulds.

fermentables.name: Calamansi
fermentables.description: Filipino sour citrus, somewhere between lime and mandarin, extremely acidic.
fermentables.usageNotes: Acid source and aromatic, not a fermentable base.

fermentables.name: Pineapple
fermentables.description: Sweet, acidic and enzymatically active — the bromelain in fresh pineapple digests protein and will strip head retention from a beer.
fermentables.usageNotes: Bromelain also degrades gelatin finings. Heat-treating deactivates it; canned pineapple is already deactivated. The base of tepache.

fermentables.name: Passionfruit
fermentables.description: Intensely aromatic and very acidic, with a low juice yield because so much of the fruit is seed and rind.
fermentables.usageNotes: A little carries a long way. Thiol-driven aroma that pairs naturally with modern hops.

fermentables.name: Guava
fermentables.description: Musky, floral and heavily pectinous. Pink varieties add colour that survives reasonably well.
fermentables.usageNotes: Very high pectin — enzyme treatment is essential or it will never clear.

fermentables.name: Banana
fermentables.description: Not juiceable in any practical sense — it is a starch-to-sugar fruit best mashed or boiled. Ripeness changes the sugar content enormously.
fermentables.usageNotes: pH 4.7 is dangerously high for a wine must; acidify. Green bananas are mostly resistant starch and need amylase.

fermentables.name: Papaya
fermentables.description: Very low acid and high pH — a papaya must sits well outside the range where wine yeast outcompetes bacteria.
fermentables.usageNotes: Papain digests protein as bromelain does. Acidify to at least pH 3.6 before pitching.

fermentables.name: Lychee
fermentables.description: High sugar, very low acid, and a rose-and-muscat aroma driven by the same terpenes found in Gewürztraminer.
fermentables.usageNotes: Acidify. The aroma is fragile — add post-fermentation.

fermentables.name: Dragonfruit
fermentables.description: Mild to the point of blandness, but the red-fleshed type contributes a startling magenta betacyanin colour.
fermentables.usageNotes: Used almost entirely for colour. The pigment is more pH-stable than anthocyanin but fades with oxygen.

fermentables.name: Jackfruit
fermentables.description: The highest-sugar fresh fruit in common use, with a heavy tropical-bubblegum aroma.
fermentables.usageNotes: Very low acid — acidification is mandatory. Laborious to process.

fermentables.name: Soursop
fermentables.description: Creamy, custard-textured pulp with a pineapple-and-cream aroma and workable natural acidity.
fermentables.usageNotes: Pulp is very thick — dilute and treat with pectic enzyme.

fermentables.name: Tamarind
fermentables.description: A dried pod pulp, not a fresh fruit: extremely high in both sugar and tartaric acid — around 10% acid by weight.
fermentables.usageNotes: One of the very few natural tartaric acid sources outside grapes. Use as a souring agent at low rates.

fermentables.name: Açaí
fermentables.description: Almost sugar-free and unusually high in fat for a fruit. Contributes colour and tannin, essentially no fermentables.
fermentables.usageNotes: The fat content will destroy head retention in beer. Colour and antioxidant only.

fermentables.name: Coconut Water
fermentables.description: Very dilute sugar with a high mineral load — potassium in particular.
fermentables.usageNotes: Contributes little gravity. Used as a partial water replacement for flavour and mouthfeel.

fermentables.name: Prickly Pear
fermentables.description: Desert cactus fruit with a brilliant betalain magenta and almost no acid at all.
fermentables.usageNotes: pH near 6 — this must be acidified aggressively or it will spoil rather than ferment. Glochids are a hazard when handling.

fermentables.name: Watermelon
fermentables.description: Over 90% water, so the gravity contribution per kilogram is among the lowest of any fruit.
fermentables.usageNotes: Acidify. The aroma is exceptionally fugitive — expect to lose most of it.

fermentables.name: Cantaloupe
fermentables.description: pH above 6 makes this one of the least safe fruits to ferment untreated.
fermentables.usageNotes: Acidify to 3.5 or below before pitching, and sulphite — the surface microflora is heavy.

fermentables.name: Honeydew
fermentables.description: As cantaloupe: high sugar for a melon, effectively no acid, and a delicate aroma.
fermentables.usageNotes: Same caution — acidify before fermenting.

fermentables.name: Raisin
fermentables.description: Dried grape: roughly 60% sugar by weight, plus the tannin, potassium and nitrogen that make it the traditional country-wine nutrient.
fermentables.usageNotes: The classic mead and country-wine body additive. Chop or the sugar stays locked inside.

fermentables.name: Date (Medjool)
fermentables.description: Among the highest-sugar foods there is — two-thirds sugar by weight, mostly already inverted.
fermentables.usageNotes: Ferments fast and clean. Low acid, so blend or acidify. The base of Middle Eastern date arak.

fermentables.name: Fig (dried)
fermentables.description: Concentrated fig sugar with a jammy, slightly resinous character.
fermentables.usageNotes: Seeds and skin can add astringency in a long maceration.

fermentables.name: Fig (fresh)
fermentables.description: Fresh figs are high in sugar and very low in acid, with a soft honeyed character.
fermentables.usageNotes: Acidify. Skin and seed give a faint tannin backbone.

fermentables.name: Prune (dried plum)
fermentables.description: Dried plum — high sugar, real acid, and a dark stewed-fruit note that suits fortified and aged styles.
fermentables.usageNotes: Contains sorbitol, so a prune ferment retains apparent sweetness.

fermentables.name: Apricot (dried)
fermentables.description: Concentrated apricot: high sugar and high acid together.
fermentables.usageNotes: Usually sulphited for colour retention — check before use if a wild or unsulphited ferment is intended.

fermentables.name: Pomegranate
fermentables.description: Punicalagin tannins give real grip, and the acid and colour are both high. One of the better standalone fruit wines.
fermentables.usageNotes: Press the arils only — the white pith is unbearably bitter.

fermentables.name: Persimmon
fermentables.description: Astringent varieties are almost unusable until fully soft, when the soluble tannin polymerises and the fruit turns sweet.
fermentables.usageNotes: Use only fully ripe fruit. pH near 5.5 demands acidification. The base of Korean gamsikcho vinegar and some soju.

fermentables.name: Kiwifruit
fermentables.description: Good natural acidity and a clean green-fruit character. Actinidin, another protease, is present.
fermentables.usageNotes: Like pineapple, it will attack gelatin finings and beer foam proteins.

fermentables.name: Rhubarb
fermentables.description: Botanically a stem, traditionally treated as fruit. Almost no sugar and a lot of acid, much of it oxalic.
fermentables.usageNotes: Use stalks only — rhubarb leaves contain enough oxalic acid to be genuinely poisonous. Always chaptalised.

fermentables.name: Pumpkin
fermentables.description: Contributes almost no fermentable sugar — a pumpkin beer tastes of spice and roast, not of pumpkin.
fermentables.usageNotes: Roast before use to develop Maillard character. Adds body and a pouring nightmare of pulp.

fermentables.name: Tomato
fermentables.description: A traditional if unfashionable country-wine base. Very low sugar, moderate acid.
fermentables.usageNotes: Requires heavy chaptalisation. The result is savoury and divides opinion sharply.

fermentables.name: Beetroot
fermentables.description: Earthy from geosmin, with a deep betalain colour and a pH high enough to be a real spoilage risk.
fermentables.usageNotes: Acidify hard. Sugar beet, the industrial relative, is the source of most European beet sugar and neutral spirit.

fermentables.name: Carrot
fermentables.description: A traditional country wine, often fortified. Low acid, low sugar, faintly sweet and earthy.
fermentables.usageNotes: Acidify and chaptalise. Best known as the base of an old-fashioned carrot whisky.

fermentables.name: Sweet Potato
fermentables.description: Mostly starch rather than sugar — the listed sugar figure understates its potential once converted.
fermentables.usageNotes: Needs a cereal mash or added amylase to convert the starch. The base of imo-jochu shochu.

fermentables.name: Agave Piña
fermentables.description: The sugar in raw agave is inulin, a fructose polymer that yeast cannot ferment. Cooking hydrolyses it to fructose.
fermentables.usageNotes: The whole-fruit sugar figure is zero on purpose: uncooked agave yields nothing. Roast or steam for 24–48 h first, then the juice runs 22–30 Brix.

fermentables.name: Apple Juice (pressed)
fermentables.description: Fresh-pressed or shelf-stable apple juice, ready to pitch. 12 Brix works out around 1.048.
fermentables.usageNotes: Check for preservatives: potassium sorbate or benzoate will stop a ferment dead. Ascorbic acid is fine.

fermentables.name: Apple Juice Concentrate
fermentables.description: Roughly 68 Brix — about six times the strength of single-strength juice.
fermentables.usageNotes: Reconstitute at about 1 part concentrate to 5 parts water for a normal cider gravity.

fermentables.name: White Grape Juice
fermentables.description: Single-strength white must at harvest gravity — around 1.092 at 22 Brix.
fermentables.usageNotes: Commercial juice is usually already sulphited; wait 24 h before pitching.

fermentables.name: Red Grape Juice
fermentables.description: Single-strength red must. Juice alone carries little tannin — that comes from skin contact.
fermentables.usageNotes: For structure, ferment on skins or add grape tannin.

fermentables.name: Grape Juice Concentrate
fermentables.description: About 68 Brix. The standard body-and-sugar addition for kit wines and a common mead adjunct.
fermentables.usageNotes: Adds tartaric acid along with the sugar — account for it before making acid corrections.

fermentables.name: Orange Juice
fermentables.description: Ferments cleanly but loses most of its aroma; the result reads more like a dry citrus wine than orange juice.
fermentables.usageNotes: Pasteurised carton juice is reliable; check for added preservatives.

fermentables.name: Pineapple Juice
fermentables.description: Canned or carton juice is heat-treated, so the bromelain problem is already solved.
fermentables.usageNotes: Unlike fresh pineapple this will not attack gelatin or beer foam.

fermentables.name: Cranberry Juice (100%)
fermentables.description: Unsweetened cranberry juice is brutally acidic — most retail 'cranberry juice' is a sweetened cocktail at a fraction of the strength.
fermentables.usageNotes: Read the label: cocktail blends are typically 25% juice and already contain sugar.

fermentables.name: Tart Cherry Concentrate
fermentables.description: About 68 Brix, and the cheapest reliable route to genuine kriek character without sourcing fresh sour cherries.
fermentables.usageNotes: Add post-fermentation to preserve aroma. Roughly 1 L per 20 L batch gives a pronounced cherry note.
